extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians designing, conducting, or evaluating measurement/instrument reliability and validation studies
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, conducting, and reporting studies that assess inter-rater and intra-rater reliability (and related validity/test-retest properties) of clinical, observational, imaging, or measurement instruments across raters, occasions, sites or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure inter-rater and intra-rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess both inter-rater reliability (agreement between different raters) and intra-rater (test-retest or within-rater) reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many studies report both (e.g., percent embolization ICC for inter- and intra-rater, Raymond Scale kappa for inter- and intra-rater). Repeated presentations of the same case/images can be used to evaluate intra-rater consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate reliability statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Select statistical measures appropriate for the data type: weighted kappa for ordinal scales, intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for continuous measures, Fleiss kappa for multiple raters, Gwet's AC1 as an alternative, percent agreement, and limits of agreement where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: use weighted kappa for the Raymond Scale (ordinal); use ICC for percent embolization (continuous); report Fleiss kappa for multi-rater image classification; report Gwet's AC1 and percent agreement for observational items; compute limits of agreement for continuous volume/measurement methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report confidence intervals and statistical uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide confidence intervals (CIs) and p-values as appropriate for reliability coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Fleiss kappa with 95% CI, ICC with confidence limits; reporting CIs helps interpret whether agreement is ‘good’, ‘fair’, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use training, consensus, and standardization to improve agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement rater training, consensus training sessions, standardized instructions, and consensus panels during instrument development and rater preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show consensus training can minimize variations (periodontal diagnosis); assemble training sets containing representative images and have expert panels provide feedback (HRME study). Reassess reliability after targeted training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include blinded evaluation when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blinded evaluators (no affiliation or knowledge of subjects' training level or other identifiers) to reduce bias in ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinded paired observers were used to evaluate surgical trainee performance, confirming interrater reliability for an OSATS assessment instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess criterion validity alongside reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instrument ratings to objective or gold-standard measures to establish criterion validity (e.g., histopathology, analgesic consumption, established scales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HRME image ratings compared with standard histopathologic analysis; CBCS-P compared with analgesic consumption and pain scores; PBCL compared with Modified Overt Aggression Scale (MOAS). Report sensitivity and specificity where classification is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate test-retest reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess stability of measures over time by repeating measurements on separate occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test-retest was used in HRIM swallow function measures and HOME FAST; report ICCs and note that test-retest reliability may vary by class of variable (e.g., contractility vs flow timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and report limits of agreement and technical error of measurement (TEM)
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing measurement methods, compute limits of agreement and TEM to quantify measurement error and interpret clinical change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disk model vs water displacement vs optoelectronic volumetry reporting limits of agreement; harmonization studies report TEMs for height and circumferences and use these when interpreting responses to treatment or follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine effects of rater experience and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether years of experience, professional background or rater type affect agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: less-experienced clinicians sometimes showed greater agreement (aneurysm embolization study); studies compared professionals, students, and trained peers for BLS assessments. Report subgroup ICCs/kappas to characterize variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze contextual and setting effects on agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether setting factors (e.g., busy ED vs quiet ED, state/hospital type, activity level) influence ratings and concordance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Australasian Triage Scale study found busy EDs yielded more urgent categories and decreased concordance; report and discuss setting-related biases and variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address prevalence and distribution effects on chance-corrected statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that unbalanced distributions of ratings can depress kappa values and misrepresent agreement beyond chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: exposure assessment study reported good concordance but low simple kappa due to unbalanced distributions. Consider reporting both percent agreement and chance-corrected measures and interpret kappa in light of prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adequate and representative samples of cases and raters
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sufficient numbers and a representative range of cases (images/patients/events) and raters to support generalizable reliability estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: studies used multiple raters (e.g., 15 neurointerventionalists, 7 HRME reviewers, 16 raters for DOSES) and dozens of cases/images; report sampling details, numbers of raters, and number of items/cases evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quality control and curated training/test materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble and use validated training sets, perform image/data quality control, and curate representative examples for rater training and testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRME study created a training set of representative images and performed image quality control prior to testing reviewers; this supports rapid training and high accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consensus processes to resolve large discrepancies and document them
rubrics_metrics.description: For retrospective assessments or when raters disagree markedly, implement and describe a consensus process to reconcile estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: industrial hygienists used a consensus process to resolve large differences before producing final exposure estimates; document how consensus was reached and how it influenced final data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report multiple complementary agreement metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report a suite of agreement metrics (percent agreement, kappa variants, ICC, sensitivity/specificity, AC1, limits of agreement) rather than a single number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different metrics capture different aspects (e.g., percent agreement vs chance-corrected agreement vs continuous agreement). Several studies presented multiple statistics to provide a fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge lower reliability for complex or subjective constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and report that complex constructs (e.g., sensationalizing, glorifying suicide) may show lower interrater reliability and may require further explication or refined operational definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: suicide reporting content analysis found highly reliable basic variables but low reliability for complicated constructs, recommending further clarification of constructs to improve measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate statistical tests to compare rater groups or conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply statistical tests suitable for the comparisons of interest (e.g., chi-square for categorical comparisons, Friedman test for related ordinal scores across conditions, ANOVA methods for reliability coefficients comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include chi-square and multirater kappa tests in periodontal consensus studies, Friedman test in triage study, and ANOVA-based techniques for intrarater/interrater reliability analysis of pneumothorax size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize measurement protocols across sites in multi-centre studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement harmonization processes (workshops, pilot studies, standard operating procedures) and evaluate inter- and intra-rater errors across centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EXERNET and other multi-centre anthropometry studies used workshops and pilot testing to achieve high reliability; report inter-rater TEMs and reliabilities across centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: When longitudinal patient assessment is required, prefer the same rater where interrater reliability is lower
rubrics_metrics.description: If intrarater reliability exceeds interrater reliability, recommend that the same assessor perform serial measurements for a given patient when feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: upper limb lymphedema study recommended the same therapist evaluate a patient because intrarater reliability was always better than interrater (except for optoelectronic method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop scales using factor analysis and validate factor structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For new scales, use exploratory (and confirmatory) factor analysis to identify dimensions and develop short/comprehensive versions, then test reliability and criterion validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem Behaviour Checklist (PBCL) used factor analysis to derive factors and then evaluated interrater reliability and sensitivity/specificity against MOAS.
